SMTO-HTTP-0045 — SMTO couldn't set up a secure connection to the service

GUID: 6c47b9b4-8a72-4b47-919e-0dc0ec7d7a2d
Slug: http-tls-handshake-failed
Domain: HTTP · Subsystem: http

What happened

  • SMTO and the service couldn't agree on how to secure the connection, so nothing was sent. The exact reason isn't known, and it doesn't mean your sign-in details are wrong.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Open Parameter Store, select the HTTP connection, and check that Base URL starts with https only if the service supports secure connections, and uses its secure port. Sending a secure request to a port that only speaks plain web traffic fails this way.
  2. Ask the service's owner whether it requires a client certificate or only accepts newer security settings. The service may refuse connections that don't meet its security requirements.
  3. If a client certificate is required, set Client certificate under TLS & transport, add the certificate and key, and save. Some services only accept connections that present an approved certificate.
  4. Select Test connection. When it shows Reachable, run the task again. The test confirms a secure connection can now be made.

What success looks like

  • Test connection shows Reachable.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to whoever runs the service; updating the Gateway's computer may be needed if it lacks newer security support. Don't set TLS verification to insecure to get past this.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The Gateway's TLS handshake failed without the client-certificate-required or certificate-verification markers, so it is classified as a general handshake failure.

What this means

  • The TLS exception lacks the recognized client-certificate-required and certificate-verification markers, so it is classified as a general handshake failure. The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.

Why this can happen

  • The TLS exception lacks the recognized client-certificate-required and certificate-verification markers, so it is classified as a general handshake failure.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect safe Gateway TLS diagnostics and server protocol/certificate configuration; the fallback does not prove a cipher mismatch.

How to fix it

  • Diagnose protocol, cipher, SNI and client-certificate compatibility from the Gateway host (for example openssl s_client -connect with -servername, -tls1_2 or -tls1_3), confirm the base_url scheme and port actually serve TLS, and adjust the server or the profile's client certificate. Do not treat it as rejected credentials or disable verification.
  • Inspect server TLS protocol, cipher and certificate compatibility. Do not treat a TLS handshake failure as rejected application credentials.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended endpoint completes a trusted TLS handshake with the supported client configuration.

What not to do

  • Do not automatically disable certificate verification or trust an unverified replacement identity.

Technical notes

  • The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.
